title: Sparse Autoencoders for Mechanistic Interpretability in NLP:A Critical Survey of Recoverability, Interpretability, and Utility

paper.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Mechanistic Interpretability in NLP: A Critical Survey of Recoverability, Interpretability, and Utility
paper.abstract:
Abstract Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising
approach to mechanistic interpretability by decomposing
language-model activations into sparse, potentially
interpretable features. However, differences in design
assumptions, evaluation objectives, and experimental
settings complicate conclusions about their effectiveness.
We present a critical survey of 138 studies on SAEs in
natural language processing. Our contributions are fourfold:
(1) we propose a task-grounded taxonomy connecting dictionary
design, feature operations, and NLP functions;
(2) we examine how sparsity allocation, geometry, data
coverage, and inference affect feature recoverability;
(3) we assess evidence for semantic interpretability,
mechanistic faithfulness, and behavioral utility; and
(4) we synthesize findings across multilingual processing,
retrieval, reasoning, classification, and behavioral
regulation, highlighting the roles of objectives, baselines,
supervision, and intervention pipelines.
Through comparative analyses of published results,
we reconcile apparent disagreements, identify unresolved
questions, and propose directions for more rigorous
evaluation. An anonymous research

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Sparse autoencoders encode model activations as sparse coefficients over a learned dictionary of feature directions ( Cunningham et al., 2024 ) . They make it possible to inspect concepts, compare representations, and intervene on internal variables at a finer granularity than whole layers or attention heads. Sparse interpretable sentence embeddings provide an earlier precedent ( Trifonov et al., 2018 ) ; transformer studies established useful feature decompositions ( Bricken et al., 2023 ; Cunningham et al., 2024 ) ; subsequent work scaled dictionaries and released reusable resources ( Templeton et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2024b ) . The scientific opportunity is now broader: can these coordinates explain how language is represented and processed, and can that understanding improve NLP systems? Answering this question requires separating four outcomes. Recoverability concerns whether an encoding procedure recovers the target latent structure, where that structure is specified. Semantic interpretability concerns whether a feature description makes discriminating predictions about activations or effects. Mechanistic faithfulness concerns whether an explanation identifies computations the original model uses. Behavioral utility concerns success on a stated task with its competing objectives. These outcomes can agree, but their definitions do not imply agreement. Consider language identity. Multilingual feature analyses use it to distinguish language-associated representations ( Deng et al., 2025 ) ; language steering seeks to induce a chosen output language ( Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) ; LangSAE removes it from pooled embeddings to improve multilingual retrieval ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . Grouping these studies simply as multilingual SAE applications hides an objective-dependent reversal: information useful for generation can be a nuisance for semantic retrieval. Conversely, grouping only by encoder architecture does not reveal this distinction at all. Existing surveys provide complementary perspectives on SAEs and mechanistic interpretability. Shu et al. (2025) synthesize SAE architectures, training procedures, feature explanations, evaluation methods, and applications. Mueller et al. (2026a) organize NLP mechanistic interpretability around causal mediators and search methods, examining which computational units and analytical procedures support explanation, hypothesis testing, and model editing. Zhang et al. (2026a) connect localization and steering to improvements in alignment, capability, and efficiency, including SAE features, task-specific metrics, and checks for unintended effects. Building on these foundations, our survey examines how SAE construction and use jointly shape the comparability and interpretation of NLP findings. This motivates three research questions. RQ1: Which design assumptions change what an SAE can recover? We compare allocation, geometry, data coverage, and inference under their stated objectives and theoretical assumptions (Section 3 ). RQ2: What evidence distinguishes an interpretable or useful feature from a faithful mechanism? We examine semantic tests, intervention controls, and counterexamples using a claim-specific rubric (Section 4 ). RQ3: Why do NLP studies reach different conclusions about SAE usefulness? We compare task objectives, supervision, and control pipelines, and reanalyse selected within-study results (Section 5 ). Our taxonomy organizes SAE studies by dictionary design, feature operation, and NLP function. Our multi-label register and comparative analyses support a task-grounded synthesis that clarifies apparent disagreements and identifies unresolved questions.

sections.text: RQ1 asks which design assumptions determine what an SAE can recover. For an NLP researcher seeking a grammatical distinction, an unsuccessful feature search leaves several explanations open: the chosen representation, the dictionary’s constraints, the training data, or the encoding procedure. sections.heading: 3.1 Defining the structure to be recovered
sections.text: The activation site determines the starting object. Residual streams contain accumulated information; attention and MLP outputs characterize component contributions. Transcoders instead approximate a component’s input–output map ( Dunefsky et al., 2024 ; Paulo et al., 2025 ) . Layer transfer, shared dictionaries, and routing change training cost and parameter reuse ( Ghilardi et al., 2024 ; Ghilardi et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) ; comparisons still need to establish what structure is preserved across sites. Within a site, the question is how that structure should be represented. Splitting distributes a concept across latents, while absorption allows a specialized latent to carry a broader property ( Chanin et al., 2025 ) ; neither supports equating an inactive coordinate with absent information. Subspace ( Engels et al., 2025 ; Dalili and Mahdavi, 2026 ) and manifold approaches ( Bhalla et al., 2026a ) model structure beyond individual directions. Nested scales ( Bussmann et al., 2025 ) , parent–child gates ( Muchane et al., 2025 ) , and Kronecker factorization ( Kurochkin et al., 2025 ) impose different forms of organization across features. Temporal smoothness ( Bhalla et al., 2026b ) and predictable-context/novelty separation ( Lubana et al., 2026 ) instead organize variation over sequences. These choices change the candidate unit of analysis: their NLP value depends on whether the resulting directions, groups, or temporal features capture the distinction under study.

sections.heading: 3.2 Allocating sparse capacity
sections.text: Once the target is specified, allocation determines which features can participate in each reconstruction. An ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty encourages sparsity but also shrinks amplitudes. Gated SAEs separate selection from magnitude estimation, while JumpReLU learns activation thresholds ( Rajamanoharan et al., 2024a ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024b ) . TopK fixes the number of retained coordinates per input ( Gao et al., 2025 ) ; BatchTopK distributes a budget across a batch and estimates an inference-time threshold ( Bussmann et al., 2024 ) . Top-AFA selects counts through a quasi-orthogonality approximation ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , AdaptiveK uses a learned complexity signal ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , and Group Bias Adaptation (GBA) targets activation-frequency coverage ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . These allocation rules make different assumptions about inputs, geometry, and feature frequency. The results show why allocation cannot be ranked by reconstruction alone. BatchTopK improves reconstruction over TopK, but its Gemma-2-2B comparison with JumpReLU is mixed for downstream cross-entropy degradation ( Bussmann et al., 2024 ) . In GBA’s variable-sparsity synthetic experiment, TopK recovery falls from 98.4% at K = 20 K=20 to 23.4% at K = 50 K=50 ; full versus misspecified frequency coverage gives GBA 100% versus 3.9% recovery ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . These rates use alignment threshold 0.9 and 128 generating features. They demonstrate sensitivity to allocation and coverage assumptions under known ground truth, rather than an NLP ranking. Comparisons should match average sparsity, data, and insertion protocol; decoder normalization must also be recorded because it changes coefficient scales (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: 3.3 Separating coverage from inference error
sections.text: Even a suitable representation and budget cannot resolve every failure. Specialized sampling and tilted risk improve access to rare concepts ( Muhamed et al., 2025b ) , changing the training distribution and emphasis of the objective. Weighted SAEs analyze recovery and reweighting under an idealized tied-weight model ( Cui et al., 2026 ) ; those assumptions delimit the result’s applicability to language-model activations. Locally amortized inference addresses a different limitation: a shared encoder can leave an optimization gap relative to per-input sparse coding ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . Improving that approximation does not establish that the reference codes are the intended linguistic features. Thus data coverage, the learning objective, and encoding accuracy require separate comparisons.

sections.heading: Answer to RQ1.
sections.text: Recoverability has separable bottlenecks: the representation and its geometry, sparse allocation, training coverage, and inference. The evidence supports diagnosing the suspected bottleneck while matching the remaining conditions. Reconstruction, recovery against a specified reference, and behavioral preservation should remain separate endpoints. Technical comparisons and assumptions are detailed in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 4.1 Testing the feature’s meaning
sections.text: A feature description is a hypothesis about its behavior. Input-oriented descriptions predict what elicits activation; output-oriented descriptions predict contributions to generation ( Gur-Arieh et al., 2025 ) . Automated explanation ( Paulo et al., 2024 ) , agentic testing ( Han et al., 2026 ) , and counterexample-guided revision ( Ma et al., 2025 ) make these hypotheses testable on held-out positives and hard negatives. The critical question is whether the description discriminates the intended property from alternatives. Descriptive collision tests whether one explanation also fits unrelated features ( McCann, 2026 ) ; contrastive stories, semantic/functional neighborhoods, and concept-separability tests examine complementary aspects of specificity ( Gulko et al., 2025 ; Mercorio et al., 2025 ; Fereidouni et al., 2026 ; Härle et al., 2025 ) . The controls must preserve what the claim says should remain invariant. A grammatical feature should track the specified contrast across appropriate lexical controls; a lexical feature need not survive word substitution. Adversarial inputs test the limits of a description ( Li et al., 2026a ) , while randomized SAE components and randomized host models challenge different sources of apparent interpretability ( Korznikov et al., 2026 ; Heap et al., 2026 ) . In the latter comparison, similar aggregate scores in several tested settings show that those metrics need not distinguish learned computations from structure present without training ( Heap et al., 2026 ) . Cross-run consistency asks whether features recur across learned dictionaries ( Song et al., 2026 ) ; recurrence alone does not validate their meaning.

sections.heading: 4.2 Testing predictive and causal effects
sections.text: A useful predictor need not identify a variable the source model uses. For a known target, SAE probes should be compared with supervised probes on the original activations, given matched information ( Kantamneni et al., 2025 ; Makelov et al., 2025 ) . For control, direct activation directions provide an alternative ( Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) . These comparisons test the benefit of the SAE representation for the chosen objective. A reusable feature vocabulary can still support exploratory discovery beyond a predefined prediction task ( Peng et al., 2025 ) . Interventions test what changes when a feature is edited. Their effects must be separated from damage introduced by reconstruction. Retaining e e isolates the decoded change but does not ensure that the edited activation lies within the model’s natural distribution. A controlled effect supports a causal claim about the manipulation; explaining the unmodified computation requires further evidence.

sections.heading: 4.3 Testing the proposed mechanism
sections.text: The gap is explicit in Makelov et al. (2024) . Their patching direction combines a concept-correlated component that is disconnected from the output with an ordinarily dormant, output-sensitive component. Patching transfers a signal between them and changes the answer through a route unused before intervention. The successful edit therefore fails to identify the natural mechanism; Appendix D.1 instantiates this counterexample. Conversely, redundant pathways can make a genuinely used feature dispensable under ablation. Necessity and sufficiency must consequently be interpreted relative to the tested interventions and contexts. A circuit claim further specifies dependencies between features. Sparse feature circuits retain feature and error nodes and test task-relevant effects ( Marks et al., 2025 ) . Module-level interventions on coactivation groups ( Deng et al., 2026 ) and transport-based feature matching ( Cao et al., 2026 ) concern group effects and correspondence. Establishing a directed circuit also requires tests of the proposed downstream dependencies; edge attribution helps select candidates for those tests. Attention-output features, formal languages, and Othello models provide distinct computational testbeds whose scope must accompany the interpretation ( Kissane et al., 2024 ; Menon et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024a ) . Neurons, heads, key–value features, and functional dictionaries offer alternative units for the computational account ( O’Neill and Bui, 2024 ; Arora et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Shafran et al., 2026 ; Dunefsky et al., 2024 ) ; the comparison should establish what the SAE basis adds.

sections.heading: Answer to RQ2.
sections.text: Semantic interpretability rests on discriminating predictions, and utility on appropriate task comparisons. Mechanistic faithfulness requires evidence that the proposed variables and dependencies capture computation the original model uses. Controlled edits contribute to that assessment, but their success alone does not establish the claimed pathway. A feature can remain useful for control even when its mechanistic interpretation fails.

sections.heading: 5 Comparing SAE Usefulness Across NLP Tasks
sections.text: RQ3 asks why NLP studies reach different conclusions about SAE usefulness. The comparison depends on what the task requires, what information the method receives, and which alternative it must outperform. We organize the findings around these differences to identify both useful contributions and the conditions under which their advantages hold. Appendix E provides extended comparisons.

sections.heading: 5.1 Objectives change the value of a feature
sections.text: Language identity makes the role of the objective explicit. LangSAE removes language-associated components from pooled multilingual-e5 embeddings for semantic retrieval, whereas CLaS-Bench edits Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to control the output language ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) . Suppressing language identity and strengthening it serve different goals. Their findings concern different task requirements. Within CLaS-Bench, residual difference-in-means scores 84.5 versus 42.3 for SAE difference-in-means, a 42.2-point gap in the combined language/relevance metric ( Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) . The reported selected settings use layers 20 and 25, respectively, both at strength 5. This establishes an advantage for the selected residual-space pipeline; differences in available layers and selection prevent isolating the SAE basis as the cause (Appendix F ). Linguistic analysis asks a more specific question than language control. Language-associated groups support observation and intervention ( Deng et al., 2025 ) ; LinguaLens tests Chinese/English linguistic contrasts ( Jing et al., 2025 ) , while TenseLoC localizes tense and tests English-feature steering ( Tumurchuluun et al., 2025 ) . Script-sensitive representations motivate matched-content and transliteration controls, with raw-neuron interventions serving as a direct comparator ( Verma et al., 2026 ) . Italian-model analysis extends coverage ( Bondielli et al., 2025 ) . Together, these studies motivate testing whether corresponding features preserve a specified linguistic contrast and intervention effect across languages; broad language selectivity or geometric similarity alone does not establish that transfer.

sections.heading: 5.2 Representations and baselines define the comparison
sections.text: Classification provides a concrete reconciliation. Positive Gemma results compare SAE classifiers with last-token hidden-state baselines ( Gallifant et al., 2025 ) . In sparse probing, adding attention-pooled dense baselines reduces the apparent advantage of pooled SAE probes ( Kantamneni et al., 2025 ) . Both studies examine pooling, so its presence alone cannot explain their disagreement. The within-study comparison establishes that baseline construction matters; attributing all cross-paper differences to it would require matching the model, data, feature selection, and classifier. Task-aligned classification additionally changes representation training ( Bail et al., 2025 ) . DILA and topic modeling construct interpretable task systems ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) , rather than explaining an unchanged source model. Speech analysis, vision–language alignment, and multimodal tracing further change the representation being examined ( Pluth et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; DHIMOÏLA et al., 2026 ; Kaushik et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . These extensions require comparisons appropriate to acoustic frames, visual embeddings, or text tokens.

sections.heading: 5.3 Information access separates RAG outcomes
sections.text: Retrieval-oriented objectives can preserve useful matching structure ( Kang et al., 2025 ) , while adapting a retriever around a frozen dictionary constructs a new retrieval system ( Formal et al., 2026 ) . For retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), improvements concern different stages: detecting unsupported output, choosing between context and memory, enriching a query, or repairing an answer. Table 2 distinguishes these operations and their information requirements. A detector can identify errors without explaining their cause, and increased reliance on context helps only when that context is trustworthy. Detect unsupported answers and guide subsequent generation. Evaluate detection and generation improvements separately. Change which information source the model relies on. Measure source preference and answer correctness separately. Query enrichment ( Abdaljalil et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) SAE-guided query modifications; some analyses select successful query expansions. Improve retrieval/generation or analyze query-expansion effects. Test on unselected queries and evaluate the contribution of the SAE within the full pipeline. Distractor repair ( Giannetti et al., 2026 ) Known correct answer token used to optimize latent activations on selected difficult examples. Recover answers affected by distracting documents. Distinguish oracle-assisted repair from autonomous error correction. Table 2: Comparison of SAE-based approaches to RAG. The methods differ in their objectives, available information, and evaluation settings; their reported improvements therefore do not measure the same capability. LatDefuse illustrates why information access belongs in the comparison. It optimizes latent edits toward a known correct token at answer divergence and evaluates distractor-vulnerable instances ( Giannetti et al., 2026 ) . The result establishes conditional repair capacity. Comparing its recovery rate directly with autonomous detection or correction would conflate different supervision and evaluation populations. An integrated system would need to evaluate detection, source arbitration, and repair together, including errors passed between stages.

sections.heading: 5.4 Selection and prompts shape instruction gains
sections.text: For reasoning, steering a strategy and identifying its computation are separate achievements. Reasoning-associated features can change traces or strategies ( Galichin et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) , while cue-injection and meaning-preserving tests can challenge an abstract-reasoning label ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . Temporal-difference analysis ties features to specified computational variables in an in-context reinforcement-learning task ( Demircan et al., 2025 ) . These findings answer different questions about control, feature meaning, and computation; lexical cues must be varied independently of the required operation to compare those claims. Instruction methods also differ in how they select features: SAIF identifies instruction-related features ( He et al., 2025 ) , narrative editing generates compliant/violating contrasts ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) , SISTER uses prompt variation ( Cho and Hockenmaier, 2025 ) , and PULSE uses labeled demonstration utility ( Hao et al., 2026 ) . Comparators need access to the same signals. Evaluation prompts matter as well: for Gemma-2-2B sentiment circuits, SST-2 F1 gains are 37.19 points under template T1 and 2.96 under T4 ( Li et al., 2026b ) . These three-run mean differences establish prompt dependence within the reported setting; they do not isolate baseline headroom as its cause. The stage of use changes the comparison further. Concept-based pretraining ( Tack et al., 2026 ) and feature-guided fine-tuning data selection ( Shi et al., 2026 ) construct changed models; transfer prediction ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) and sparse model diffing ( Kassem et al., 2025 ) respectively anticipate and diagnose updates. Inference-time activation or input edits leave weights fixed; diffusion-language analyses additionally depend on denoising time and mask position ( Wang et al., 2026b ) .

sections.heading: 5.5 Controllers determine regulation trade-offs
sections.text: Behavioral regulation tests what the complete intervention achieves. Refusal-feature analysis and adversarial detection ( Yeo et al., 2025 ) concern different outcomes from maintaining benign capabilities during control. Static refusal amplification can impair unrelated capabilities ( O’Brien et al., 2024 ) ; REINS and graph-regularized steering combine selected directions with runtime gating ( Ding et al., 2026 ; Yeon et al., 2025 ) . Their comparison therefore involves both the feature directions and the decision about when to intervene. Unlearning makes this distinction concrete. Static suppression has mixed multi-topic results ( Farrell et al., 2024 ) ; Dynamic SAE Guardrails add input-dependent classification ( Muhamed et al., 2025a ) , whereas subspace-guided projection and CRISP modify parameters ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Ashuach et al., 2026 ) . Conditional intervention can avoid unnecessary edits, while parameter updates remove dependence on a runtime controller. Comparing their forget–retain trade-offs requires matching target knowledge, evaluation populations, retention tasks, and relearning attacks. Adaptation constraints ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Peng et al., 2026 ) and backdoor analyses ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Antoun et al., 2026 ) add further training and attack conditions. These differences identify what a controlled comparison must hold fixed before attributing a gain to the dictionary.

sections.heading: Answer to RQ3.
sections.text: SAE usefulness depends on the objective, representation, comparison baseline, available supervision, and intervention pipeline. Opposing treatments of language identity can both serve their respective tasks; classification, repair, and regulation results require matching the conditions defining success. The synthesis reconciles the scope of these findings. Establishing which factor causes a remaining performance difference requires experiments that vary it while controlling the others.

sections.heading: 6 Research Directions and Practical Choices
sections.text: The answers to RQ1–RQ3 identify recovery bottlenecks, requirements for mechanistic claims, and conditions shaping task utility. They motivate experiments that distinguish competing explanations and guide the choice of an appropriate unit of analysis.

sections.heading: Discourse structure versus temporal persistence.
sections.text: Compare static and temporal dictionaries with matched host model, layer, capacity, average sparsity, and training corpus ( Bhalla et al., 2026b ; Lubana et al., 2026 ) . Vary semantic continuity, lexical repetition, and abrupt discourse change independently. Measure held-out contrast discrimination and predicted intervention effects on entity/state tracking. This tests whether temporal structure captures discourse-relevant distinctions beyond lexical persistence; smooth codes and separate task gains would leave that relationship unresolved.

sections.heading: Feature matching versus intervention transfer.
sections.text: Match features across random seeds, paraphrases, and languages using geometry and activation distributions, then test whether correspondence predicts preservation of an independently specified intervention effect. Include unmatched and frequency-matched controls. Current consistency and matching measures ( Song et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2026 ) motivate these comparisons, while known-concept disentanglement results ( Mueller et al., 2026b ) motivate testing functional roles separately.

sections.heading: Selection and controller versus dictionary.
sections.text: With fixed train/validation/test splits, cross SAE dictionaries with shared supervised or unsupervised selection rules and static or gated controllers. Include dense probes for prediction and direct-space directions for control, with matched labels and tuning budgets. Report the target–retention frontier. The probing/classification disagreement and conditional-control advances motivate this design; attributing their differences to selection or gating remains a hypothesis until those factors are controlled.

sections.heading: 6.2 Choosing when an SAE adds value
sections.text: For a known predictive target, begin with a well-tuned supervised probe and a matched label budget. For output control, include direct activation directions before incurring dictionary-training and feature-selection costs. For a localized computational hypothesis, neurons, heads, or a functional surrogate may provide the required unit. Direct comparators support these choices ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Arora et al., 2026 ; Shafran et al., 2026 ; Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) . An SAE is more compelling when a reusable, fine-grained feature vocabulary enables discovery, comparison across many questions, or a demonstrated specificity/cost advantage.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: This survey critically examines the role of sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability and NLP. Through a task-grounded taxonomy of dictionary design, feature operations, and NLP functions, we identify key challenges in feature recoverability, distinguish semantic interpretability from mechanistic faithfulness, and explain how task objectives and experimental pipelines shape reported utility. Our comparative synthesis reconciles apparent disagreements across studies and highlights where matched evaluations remain necessary. These findings provide NLP researchers with a framework for evaluating SAE contributions, selecting appropriate baselines, and determining whether useful features also explain the model’s underlying computations.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: This survey focuses on sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability and their applications to natural language processing. It does not aim to comprehensively cover related developments in sparse coding, disentangled representation learning, or interpretability methods beyond SAEs. Given the rapid evolution of this research area, our synthesis reflects the literature available within the survey’s defined scope. Comparisons across studies are constrained by differences in model architectures, datasets, feature representations, and evaluation protocols. Accordingly, our analyses emphasize the conditions under which findings are supported rather than establishing universal rankings of SAE methods. The proposed taxonomy and evidence framework provide a basis for future comparative evaluations, including controlled experiments across NLP tasks.

sections.heading: Appendix A Survey Methodology and Reproducibility
sections.text: We conducted a structured critical survey of SAE methods and their applications to language-model analysis and NLP system construction, including relevant speech and multimodal extensions. The literature search focused on sparse autoencoders , dictionary learning , mechanistic interpretability , language models , feature circuits , and activation steering . We consulted Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, and the ACL Anthology, covering publications primarily from 2024 to 2026 in ACL, EMNLP, ICLR, NeurIPS, ICML, and related venues, including Findings papers, with a literature cutoff of 12 October 2026. Figure 2 summarizes the included studies by reference-version year. Conference proceedings, PMLR, arXiv, and OpenReview were also consulted to identify and verify relevant studies and publication versions. Of the 199 records collected, five duplicate or overlapping version pairs were merged, yielding 194 unique candidates. Following scope and source verification, 138 studies were included. Six additional methodological anchors and four background works informed the discussion but were excluded from the study-frequency counts. Each included study was classified according to dictionary design, feature operation, and NLP function, with relevant experimental settings and source references retained. The anonymous research register linked in the abstract provides the study records, coding guide, selection decisions, source-level evidence ledger, numerical extractions, and reproduction script as pages and individual files. Reported findings are distinguished from our interpretations. 2023 2024 2025 2026 Linguistic structure 0 0 5 3 Dictionary design 1 5 12 10 Text analysis 0 1 5 2 Knowledge/retrieval 0 1 5 6 Feature methodology 0 4 13 16 Circuits/reasoning 0 5 6 9 Safety/alignment 0 2 6 9 Speech/multimodal 0 0 1 11 Figure 2: Year of the selected reference version, after publication-metadata corrections. sections.text: For study s s , T ⁡ ( s ) = ( D s , O s , F s , Z s ) T(s)=(D_{s},O_{s},F_{s};Z_{s}) records dictionary design, feature operation, and NLP function, with model/site, supervision, selection, intervention, and source-version qualifiers in Z s Z_{s} . Table 3 defines the labels and assignment boundaries. Labels describe source-supported contributions retained in the synthesis; multiple labels preserve overlap, while an absent secondary label denotes an unextracted contribution. The facets can interact and are not assumed statistically independent. Code Category Assignment criterion Boundary or clarification Dictionary design (D) A Adopted/comparative Uses or compares an existing dictionary; dictionary construction is not the main contribution. Does not imply a new SAE architecture. B Budget/amplitude Changes sparsity allocation or separates feature selection from activation magnitude. Using a TopK checkpoint alone does not qualify. G Geometry/structure Changes feature geometry, grouping, hierarchy, signs, or relational constraints. A semantic label does not establish a multidimensional representation. C Coverage/objective Changes training-data coverage or the objective determining what is preserved. Task-specific supervision is recorded separately. I Inference/site/sharing Changes sparse-code inference, activation sites, or parameter sharing. Choosing a layer for an application is not necessarily a design contribution. F Functional/alternative Uses a functional surrogate, alternative basis, or direct representation as a comparator. Transcoders model input–output mappings, not same-state reconstruction. Feature operation (O) D Describe/characterize Analyzes features, representations, reconstruction, or interpretability. A feature description does not establish a natural computational mechanism. P Predict/diagnose Uses features to predict outcomes or diagnose observed changes. Predictive association does not establish causation. T Trace dependencies Identifies or tests directed computational dependencies or algorithmic relationships. Undirected coactivation alone is insufficient. Using a language model alone does not establish a linguistic contribution. K Knowledge/retrieval Studies retrieval, source reliance, context use, or unsupported answers. Knowledge unlearning is primarily behavioral regulation. R Reasoning/adaptation Studies reasoning, instruction following, transfer, or model adaptation. Distinguish changes to weights, inputs, and runtime activations. S Behavioral regulation Studies refusal, bias, unlearning, adversarial behavior, or safety control. A narrow safety result does not establish general safety. A Text analytics Studies classification, topic modeling, text provenance, or text-based analysis. sections.heading: C.2 Identifiability and the object represented
sections.text: The linear representation hypothesis concerns representing a concept through a direction or low-dimensional linear structure ( Park et al., 2024 ) . Superposition concerns encoding more features than available dimensions using overlapping directions. Neither assumption by itself guarantees that a particular learned dictionary uniquely recovers the intended concepts. A low reconstruction error means the selected codes reproduce activations under a metric. It does not guarantee that a unique dictionary is identifiable from that distribution. Permutation/scaling symmetries are elementary ambiguities; correlated or hierarchical factors can support substantively different decompositions. Ground-truth recovery is measurable in synthetic settings with a known generating dictionary. In a natural LM, semantic tests, controlled tasks, and functional comparisons provide partial constraints, rather than direct access to an agreed ground-truth feature inventory. Splitting represents a nominal concept through multiple latents, sometimes at different granularities. Absorption occurs when a specialized feature also carries a more general property, so absence of the nominal general feature’s activation does not imply absence of that information ( Chanin et al., 2025 ) . Composition concerns how multiple factors combine to represent or compute a target; KronSAE’s factorized interactions implement a different assumption from either phenomenon ( Kurochkin et al., 2025 ) . Ablating one split coordinate may underestimate distributed involvement; ablating an absorbing coordinate can affect several semantic properties. These are reasons to inspect feature sets and their side effects, not to assume every feature group is a causal mechanism. A multidimensional concept occupies a subspace or requires several coordinates ( Engels et al., 2025 ; Dalili and Mahdavi, 2026 ) . A concept manifold introduces continuous geometry that may be represented by global spanning features or local tiling ( Bhalla et al., 2026a ) . Matryoshka dictionaries couple nested reconstruction scales ( Bussmann et al., 2025 ) ; hierarchical gating models explicit parent–child dependence ( Muchane et al., 2025 ) ; cascaded SAE++ learns higher-level concepts over decoder directions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . These differences determine what an intervention on a node, group, prefix, or subspace means. The rate–distortion–polysemanticity model further shows why co-occurrence can change the preferred decomposition ( Mencattini et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: C.3 Sequence, coverage, and computational site
sections.text: Temporal smoothness and predictable-context decomposition are different hypotheses about sequences ( Bhalla et al., 2026b ; Lubana et al., 2026 ) . The former favors slowly changing higher-level factors; the latter separates predictable information from novelty. Neither supplies semantic ground truth: repeated lexical forms can be temporally stable, and a linguistically important contrast can be predictable. A discourse experiment should independently vary semantic continuity, lexical repetition, and information novelty, measuring both feature organization and intervention effects. Coverage is an independent source of failure. A concept absent or extremely rare in the training activations cannot be recovered as reliably as one repeatedly represented in appropriate contexts. Specialized SAEs change sampling and risk weighting ( Muhamed et al., 2025b ) ; multilingual coverage adds language, script, tokenization, and construction-frequency imbalances. General-purpose and specialized dictionaries should be compared with their different data and supervision budgets visible. An apparent architectural advantage can otherwise be a coverage advantage. Residual-stream SAEs characterize a mixed running state; attention-output SAEs expose context-dependent writes; MLP-output SAEs characterize another update to that state. A transcoder learns a sparse approximation to an input–output function, creating a different candidate causal object. A pooled-embedding SAE for retrieval collapses token position and belongs to a different representation level. Speech frames, visual tokens, and diffusion timestep/mask position introduce further indexing variables.

sections.heading: D.2 Reconstruction, distribution shift, and edges
sections.text: Equation 2 preserves the original reconstruction residual. A null edit z ′ = z z^{\prime}=z then returns the original activation, while replacing it with the decoded reconstruction can alter the model before any intended edit occurs. This distinguishes reconstruction damage from the effect of the feature delta. It does not ensure that the edited state was naturally reachable. Large coefficients, incompatible coactivation, or simultaneous edits across sites can create off-manifold states. Matched-norm random directions, naturally occurring replacement values, coefficient sweeps, retention tasks, and token-level effects probe different confounds. They should be selected for the claim rather than applied as an undifferentiated checklist. A failed off-target test may weaken specificity while leaving a target causal effect intact. A null necessity result can reflect redundant computation; it does not by itself prove irrelevance. Sufficiency is likewise conditional on the receiving context and intervention convention. An edge in a circuit diagram should state its construction: activation correlation, geometric matching, gradient-based attribution, or intervention-confirmed dependence. These are not interchangeable. Attribution can prioritize candidate edges efficiently, while controlled removal/restoration and counterfactual tests assess whether the selected path supports the task. Transcoder reconstruction of a component function and SAE reconstruction of one state have different error terms; a circuit comparison must retain those differences.

sections.heading: Appendix E Deep Comparative NLP Cases
sections.text: These cases extend RQ3 by comparing representations, objectives, and intervention pipelines. Numerical contrasts are examined in Appendix F ; selected source observations and their interpretations are documented in Appendix G .

sections.heading: E.1 Linguistic identity, grammatical variables, and transfer
sections.text: The multilingual literature moves through several distinct objects. Language-associated groups ( Deng et al., 2025 ) concern broad selectivity and combined interventions. LinguaLens constructs counterfactual contrasts and tests ablation/enhancement on Llama-3.1-8B with OpenSAE checkpoints; its causal estimates depend on the selected examples and LLM-judged outcome ( Jing et al., 2025 ) . TenseLoC distinguishes locating an attention-output bottleneck from steering selected residual-stream SAE features ( Tumurchuluun et al., 2025 ) . Script-controlled analysis demonstrates why broad language associations may track writing systems; its raw-neuron interventions belong to a direct-comparator role ( Verma et al., 2026 ) . The comparison suggests an ordered set of questions, not an evidence hierarchy across papers. First identify what varies: language identity, script, tense, meaning, or discourse role. Then hold matched semantic content where possible, use minimal grammatical contrasts, and test paraphrase or transliteration when the claim predicts invariance. Finally assess whether a matched feature preserves the predicted intervention effect across languages. Vector similarity alone does not establish that equivalence. Evidence from Italian models ( Bondielli et al., 2025 ) and the studied multilingual sets establishes broader coverage than English-only discovery. It does not justify an extrapolation to all low-resource languages or morphologically diverse systems. Tokenization, script, corpus frequency, and syntactic constructions can each change the learned decomposition. A useful next comparison samples these factors explicitly and reports per-language semantic and functional outcomes rather than only a macro-average.

sections.heading: E.2 Language identity as a target and as a nuisance
sections.text: LangSAE uses a frozen multilingual-e5-large encoder, mean-pooled 1,024-dimensional representations, and a TopK-style sparse dictionary; it removes language-associated components before normalized retrieval scoring ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . Its training construction draws on mMARCO and MIRACL in ten languages. The question is whether the edited representation preserves semantic query–document relations while reducing an unwanted language cue. CLaS-Bench instead studies output-language control in an autoregressive instruction model ( Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) . A language cue that is undesirable for language-invariant retrieval is now the target signal. The source compares direct residual methods, probes, and SAE-derived directions under method-specific settings. Its mean score combines language fidelity and response relevance, and SAE comparisons are limited to layers with available checkpoints. Consequently, the observed direct-space advantage does not isolate dictionary quality from layer availability and selection procedure. The common term “language feature” conceals these opposite objectives and different representation sites.

sections.heading: E.3 Prediction versus construction in sparse classification
sections.text: Kantamneni et al. (2025) evaluate sparse probes on Gemma-2-9B with JumpReLU GemmaScope dictionaries, with a Llama-3.1-8B/TopK replication. They examine last-token and multi-token max-pooled representations, attention-pooled dense baselines, and feature binarization. Gallifant et al. (2025) use frozen Gemma-family models and public dictionaries, vary pooling and binarization, and train logistic regression with five-fold cross-validation. Their neural baseline uses last-token hidden states. Bail et al. (2025) instead align representations to classification tasks; their encoder-only and decoder-only models also use different extraction sites. Source observation: the within-study baseline comparison in Kantamneni et al. (2025) reduces the apparent pooled-SAE advantage when attention-pooled dense probes are available. This provides direct evidence that baseline construction matters in that protocol. Survey interpretation: positive classification results and limited generic-probing gains need not contradict each other because the representation, aggregation, selected features, classifier, and baseline differ. It would be inaccurate to attribute the difference simply to one paper using pooling and the other omitting it. Nor does this comparison isolate the cause of every difference between Gallifant et al. (2025) ; Kantamneni et al. (2025) ; Bail et al. (2025) . A matched study should fix model, layer, dataset split, label and tuning budgets while varying pooling, feature selection, task alignment, and head capacity.

sections.heading: E.4 RAG: detection, source arbitration, and oracle repair
sections.text: Table 2 summarizes the stage and information requirements underlying these comparisons. Dense embedding decomposition ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ) and retrieval-oriented objectives ( Kang et al., 2025 ; Formal et al., 2026 ) can produce controllable representations. Query-expansion feature discovery selects 2,000 pairs that improve MRR@10 ( Dong et al., 2026 ) . The source also analyzes helpful, neutral, and harmful expansions (their Appendix B.2); this broader diagnostic analysis does not remove the success-conditioned selection of steering latents. SAFE integrates feature signals into query enrichment and subsequent generation ( Abdaljalil et al., 2025 ) . All of these are system-level contributions whose SAE-specific benefit requires a pipeline ablation. HalluSAE and RAGLens predict hallucination-related outcomes ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Xiong et al., 2026 ) . RAGLens evaluates Llama2-7B/13B on RAGTruth and Dolly and tests additional model/dataset combinations; its detector and feedback stage are separate evaluations. Re-encoding through another backbone is not evidence that identical latent indices or meanings transfer. Sparse-latent source arbitration in Llama-3.1-8B ( Xin et al., 2025 ) and SPARE ( Zhao et al., 2025b ) instead changes reliance on context or internal knowledge. A proper correctness analysis must cross the intervention with whether each source is trustworthy. LatDefuse selects distractor-vulnerable BioASQ, Natural Questions, and PopQA cases, then optimizes latent activations toward the known correct token at the first answer divergence ( Giannetti et al., 2026 ) . Both the host model and SAE remain frozen. The selected population contains approximately 255 instances per model, with gold context between two hard distractors. Its DCD/MDR decoding baselines also use oracle information—gold versus distractor document roles—but this is different from the correct-token optimization target. Source observation: optimized edits restore answers in this selected setting. Survey interpretation: this establishes conditional repair capacity, not autonomous error detection or correction; post-hoc feature labels do not uniquely identify a natural semantic mechanism. The source acknowledges supervision and semantic-interpretation limits. Its Llama naming remains inconsistent: its Section 4.1 and footnote 2 name Llama-3-8B, while its Table 1 and SAE checkpoint name Llama-3.1-8B. We retain that unresolved discrepancy in the ledger and use the unambiguous Gemma-2-2B setting for concrete model examples.

sections.heading: E.5 Reasoning and instruction: labels, cues, and supervision
sections.text: Reasoning steering ( Galichin et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) and reasoning-feature falsification ( Ma et al., 2026 ) concern different propositions. A feature can help induce a strategy while responding to a phrase rather than an abstract operation. Meaning-preserving rewrites and cue insertion test the semantic label; controlled reasoning tasks and targeted counterfactuals test the computational interpretation. Temporal-difference analysis supplies explicit reward/value/error variables in a specified in-context reinforcement-learning task ( Demircan et al., 2025 ) ; it should not be described as a temporal SAE architecture or as general evidence about chain-of-thought reasoning. For instruction following, generated compliant/violating narrative contrasts ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) , prompt-variation feature selection ( Cho and Hockenmaier, 2025 ) , instruction-associated latents ( He et al., 2025 ) , and labeled demonstration utility ( Hao et al., 2026 ) provide different information to the method. A comparison that grants a known target to one selector and only an unsupervised label to another does not isolate representation quality. In sentiment circuits, the same intervention has markedly different gains across prompt templates ( Li et al., 2026b ) ; this motivates reporting the prompt baseline as part of the method’s information and evaluation context. CoCoMix changes pretraining by predicting and interleaving SAE-derived concepts ( Tack et al., 2026 ) ; IGDS selects fine-tuning data using feature recall and intervention-based relevance ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . Transfer prediction uses pre-update signals ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , whereas MNEME diagnoses changes after an update ( Kassem et al., 2025 ) . These stages have distinct prediction targets and access to labels or updated weights. Input optimization and inference-time activation edits are not weight adaptation. Diffusion-language work additionally conditions its feature interpretation on timestep and mask state ( Wang et al., 2026b ) .

sections.heading: E.6 Safety and unlearning: location, conditionality, persistence
sections.text: Feature discovery, adversarial detection, and control should be extracted as separate claims. Constant refusal amplification has an observable target/benign-utility trade-off ( O’Brien et al., 2024 ) . REINS uses harmful-feature suppression, refusal enhancement, and gating on Qwen3.5 base models ( Ding et al., 2026 ) ; graph-regularized steering also combines structured directions with a runtime decision ( Yeon et al., 2025 ) . These are composite controllers, so an improvement over static steering need not be an improvement in feature semantics. Early SAE unlearning evaluates selected knowledge and has mixed multi-topic results ( Farrell et al., 2024 ) . Dynamic SAE Guardrails use Gemma-2-2B-it with a layer-3 residual SAE and input-dependent feature statistics ( Muhamed et al., 2025a ) . SSPU and CRISP change parameters using SAE-derived constraints ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Ashuach et al., 2026 ) . The former runtime gate can avoid acting on unrelated inputs; persistent parameter changes eliminate that particular runtime dependency but create a different forgetting/retention and relearning problem. We compare where the change resides and what information selects it; a pooled ranking across unmatched benchmark denominators would hide these differences. Reward modeling ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , low-rank adaptation ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , and coupled constraints during fine-tuning ( Peng et al., 2026 ) construct interpretable or constrained training systems. Emergent-misalignment geometry ( Minegishi et al., 2026 ) , medical-bias steering ( Ayadi and Hautli-Janisz, 2026 ) , and fine-grained safety resources ( Weng et al., 2026 ) add domain-specific diagnostic and control targets. Backdoor analyses find different roles for trigger detection, propagation, and output control across attack constructions and sites ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Antoun et al., 2026 ) . These results motivate reporting the attack and benign population, not extrapolating a narrow diagnostic success to general safety.

sections.heading: E.7 Text analytics, speech, and multimodal extensions
sections.text: Company similarity ( Molinari et al., 2025 ) , artificial-text detection ( Kuznetsov et al., 2025 ) , medical coding ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , classification ( Bail et al., 2025 ) , and topic modeling ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) use sparse features to construct or explain task systems. Watermark sampling ( Yu et al., 2025 ) and text-based confounding adjustment ( Zhong et al., 2026 ) have still different targets. In the latter, causal adjustment concerns an external data-generating question, not necessarily the language model’s internal causal mechanism. These studies remain in the map to mark the boundary between interpretable system construction and source-model explanation. Whisper analysis operates on acoustic encoder frames rather than text-token residual states ( Pluth et al., 2026 ) . Cross-modal feature heterogeneity, energy alignment, and group-sparse dictionaries test how text and visual representations share or separate concepts ( Lee et al., 2026 ; DHIMOÏLA et al., 2026 ; Kaushik et al., 2026 ) . Hierarchical CLIP features and cascaded SAE++ introduce further structural objects ( Zaigrajew et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) ; multimodal circuit tracing models input–output dependencies using transcoders ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . A semantic label can be shared while directions or causal roles differ, so text-only geometric conclusions do not transfer automatically. Other extensions construct systems: sparse-feature distribution matching selects image-caption training data ( Das et al., 2026 ) , concept coverage guides token pruning ( Li et al., 2026c ) , and caption-conditioned masks alter visual representations for retrieval ( Mahajan et al., 2026 ) . Representation analysis motivates multimodal retrieval realignment ( Feng et al., 2026 ) ; text-derived visual steering also contains non-SAE alternatives, whose gains must not be attributed wholly to SAEs ( Gan et al., 2026 ) . These cases test representation portability and objective dependence, while their specific accuracy or retrieval outcomes remain modality- and protocol-dependent.

Each case separates the published result from our interpretation.

sections.heading: E02. Recovery depends on frequency coverage
sections.text: Source and setting: Chen et al. (2026b) : a synthetic dictionary with uniform marginal feature frequencies and variable sample sparsity (Appendix F.4 ). Observation: at alignment threshold 0.9, TopK recovery is 98.4/24.2/23.4% for K = 20 / 30 / 50 K=20/30/50 ; GBA reaches 100% with full target-frequency coverage and 3.9% when coverage excludes the generating frequency. Interpretation: sparsity allocation and specified frequency coverage change recovery in this known model. The comparison does not measure long-tail linguistic recovery or NLP accuracy.

sections.heading: E10. Direct-space steering can outperform SAE steering
sections.text: Source and setting: Gurgurov et al. (2026) : CLaS-Bench on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across 32 languages (Appendix F.2 ). Observation: residual and SAE DiffMean score 84.5 and 42.3. The reported selected settings use layers 20/25, respectively, with strength 5; the source prose instead gives an SAE peak at strength 15. This discrepancy remains unresolved. Interpretation: the result favors the selected residual pipeline; it does not isolate dictionary quality from selection and available layers. The SAE edit restores the reconstruction residual, excluding simple reconstruction replacement as an explanation of the gap.

sections.heading: E11. Sparse-probe gains depend on the baseline
sections.text: Source and setting: Kantamneni et al. (2025) : Gemma-2-9B/JumpReLU GemmaScope, with a Llama-3.1-8B/TopK replication. Observation: providing attention-pooled dense probes reduces the apparent advantage of max-pooled SAE probes; the source also examines binarization. Interpretation: baseline construction matters within this protocol. Both compared classification studies examine pooling, so its mere presence cannot reconcile their findings. Appendix E.3 separates the remaining differences in representation, feature selection, supervision, and classifier capacity.

sections.heading: E16. Latent optimization establishes conditional repair
sections.text: Source and setting: Giannetti et al. (2026) : frozen models and dictionaries, approximately 255 distractor-vulnerable examples per model (Appendix E.4 ). Observation: optimizing latents toward the correct token recovers answers in this selected population. DCD/MDR comparators instead use oracle document roles. Gemma-2-2B is unambiguous; Llama model naming differs between methods and result labels. Interpretation: these results establish answer-conditioned repair capacity. They do not evaluate autonomous detection/correction, and post-hoc feature labels do not uniquely identify the natural mechanism.

sections.heading: E17. Sentiment gains vary with the prompt
sections.text: Source and setting: Li et al. (2026b) : Gemma-2-2B, SST-2, GemmaScope dictionaries, validation-calibrated circuit amplification, and first-output-token classification (Appendix F.1 ). Observation: three-run mean F1 gains across T1–T4 are 37.19, 14.99, 6.28, and 2.96 percentage points. Interpretation: the measured benefit is prompt-dependent; baseline headroom is not isolated as its cause. Zero-shot prompting does not imply unsupervised circuit discovery or strength selection. The extracted means provide no dispersion for significance testing.

sections.heading: E20. Counterexamples refine feature descriptions
sections.text: Source and setting: Ma et al. (2025) , methods on feature sampling, explanation, activation simulation, and revision: selected features from Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GPT-2 Small, assessed with held-out and synthetic tests. Observation: mismatches between description-predicted and observed activation reveal failures in initial explanations and guide revisions. Interpretation: this supports a falsifiable description workflow. Description accuracy does not establish a computational role, consistent with the claim distinctions in Table 1 and Appendix D .
