Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.20139v1 [cs.CL] 14 Oct 2026 Sparse Autoencoders for Mechanistic Interpretability in NLP: A Critical Survey of Recoverability, Interpretability, and Utility Salima Lamsiyah Adelaide Danilov Affiliation: Oleksandr Marchenko Breneur Aria Nourbakhsh Affiliation: Department of Computer Science (DCS), University of Luxembourg Affiliation: Correspondence: salima.lamsiyah@uni.lu Abstract Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach to mechanistic interpretability by decomposing language-model activations into sparse, potentially interpretable features. However, differences in design assumptions, evaluation objectives, and experimental settings complicate conclusions about their effectiveness. We present a critical survey of 138 studies on SAEs in natural language processing. Our contributions are fourfold: (1) we propose a task-grounded taxonomy connecting dictionary design, feature operations, and NLP functions; (2) we examine how sparsity allocation, geometry, data coverage, and inference affect feature recoverability; (3) we assess evidence for semantic interpretability, mechanistic faithfulness, and behavioral utility; and (4) we synthesize findings across multilingual processing, retrieval, reasoning, classification, and behavioral regulation, highlighting the roles of objectives, baselines, supervision, and intervention pipelines. Through comparative analyses of published results, we reconcile apparent disagreements, identify unresolved questions, and propose directions for more rigorous evaluation. An anonymous research register 1 1 1 https://anonymous.4open.science/r/sae-research-register-C331/register.html accompanies the survey. 1 Introduction Sparse autoencoders encode model activations as sparse coefficients over a learned dictionary of feature directions ( Cunningham et al., 2024 ) . They make it possible to inspect concepts, compare representations, and intervene on internal variables at a finer granularity than whole layers or attention heads. Sparse interpretable sentence embeddings provide an earlier precedent ( Trifonov et al., 2018 ) ; transformer studies established useful feature decompositions ( Bricken et al., 2023 ; Cunningham et al., 2024 ) ; subsequent work scaled dictionaries and released reusable resources ( Templeton et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2024b ) . The scientific opportunity is now broader: can these coordinates explain how language is represented and processed, and can that understanding improve NLP systems? Answering this question requires separating four outcomes. Recoverability concerns whether an encoding procedure recovers the target latent structure, where that structure is specified. Semantic interpretability concerns whether a feature description makes discriminating predictions about activations or effects. Mechanistic faithfulness concerns whether an explanation identifies computations the original model uses. Behavioral utility concerns success on a stated task with its competing objectives. These outcomes can agree, but their definitions do not imply agreement. Consider language identity. Multilingual feature analyses use it to distinguish language-associated representations ( Deng et al., 2025 ) ; language steering seeks to induce a chosen output language ( Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) ; LangSAE removes it from pooled embeddings to improve multilingual retrieval ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . Grouping these studies simply as multilingual SAE applications hides an objective-dependent reversal: information useful for generation can be a nuisance for semantic retrieval. Conversely, grouping only by encoder architecture does not reveal this distinction at all. Existing surveys provide complementary perspectives on SAEs and mechanistic interpretability. Shu et al. (2025) synthesize SAE architectures, training procedures, feature explanations, evaluation methods, and applications. Mueller et al. (2026a) organize NLP mechanistic interpretability around causal mediators and search methods, examining which computational units and analytical procedures support explanation, hypothesis testing, and model editing. Zhang et al. (2026a) connect localization and steering to improvements in alignment, capability, and efficiency, including SAE features, task-specific metrics, and checks for unintended effects. Building on these foundations, our survey examines how SAE construction and use jointly shape the comparability and interpretation of NLP findings. This motivates three research questions. RQ1: Which design assumptions change what an SAE can recover? We compare allocation, geometry, data coverage, and inference under their stated objectives and theoretical assumptions (Section 3 ). RQ2: What evidence distinguishes an interpretable or useful feature from a faithful mechanism? We examine semantic tests, intervention controls, and counterexamples using a claim-specific rubric (Section 4 ). RQ3: Why do NLP studies reach different conclusions about SAE usefulness? We compare task objectives, supervision, and control pipelines, and reanalyse selected within-study results (Section 5 ). Our taxonomy organizes SAE studies by dictionary design, feature operation, and NLP function. Our multi-label register and comparative analyses support a task-grounded synthesis that clarifies apparent disagreements and identifies unresolved questions. 2 Scope and Organizing Framework We survey SAE methods for language-model analysis and NLP system construction, including relevant speech and multimodal extensions. Corpus selection and coding are detailed in Appendix A . Dictionary design Which feature object is obtained? Sparsity allocation; geometry Training objective and coverage Inference and activation site Functional alternatives Feature operation What is done with the features? Describe / characterize Predict / diagnose Trace dependencies Edit / construct NLP function Which objective defines success? Linguistic distinctions Knowledge / retrieval Reasoning, instruction, adaptation Behavioral regulation Specify the comparison: feature object + operation + NLP objective Retain model/version, activation site, data, supervision, feature selection, and intervention protocol. Claim-dependent evidence: choose tests for the claim Recoverability Reference latent structure; recovery criteria and stated assumptions Semantic interpretability Held-out contrasts; hard negatives; feature discrimination Mechanistic faithfulness Controlled interventions; reconstruction controls; natural-pathway evidence Behavioral utility Matched task baselines; retention and side effects; generalization Figure 1: Three facets jointly define a comparison (top), interpreted alongside its experimental settings (middle). Complementary evidence targets assess what the findings support (bottom). Arrows show how the facets inform study comparison and claim assessment; the tests are illustrative and tailored to the claim. Three facets and their qualifiers. For study s s , we record T ⁡ ( s ) = ( D s , O s , F s , Z s ) T(s)=(D_{s},O_{s},F_{s};Z_{s}) (Figure 1 ). Dictionary design D s D_{s} describes how features are obtained or constrained: sparsity allocation, geometry, coverage and objectives, inference and activation sites, or functional alternatives. Feature operation O s O_{s} describes their use: characterize representations, predict or diagnose outcomes, trace dependencies, or edit model behavior and construct systems. NLP function F s F_{s} specifies the evaluation target, covering linguistic distinctions, knowledge and retrieval, reasoning and adaptation, behavioral regulation, text analytics, speech and multimodal analysis, and general enabling research. The facets interact: a task can shape dictionary training, while dictionary structure can enable particular operations. Qualifiers Z s Z_{s} retain model/version, activation site, data, supervision, feature selection, and intervention protocol. Together, the upper boxes and central band in Figure 1 expose differences in experimental settings that may explain apparent disagreements. Claim-dependent evidence. The taxonomy identifies comparable studies; the evidence framework assesses their claims. In the lower row of Figure 1 , claims about feature recoverability, semantic interpretability, mechanistic faithfulness, and behavioral utility require different tests and controls. In particular, demonstrating the utility of SAE-derived features in a classifier, retriever, or controller does not necessarily establish the computations performed by the original model. The operational definitions, study assignments, and cross-dimensional analyses are provided in Appendix B . 3 Dictionary Design and Recoverability RQ1 asks which design assumptions determine what an SAE can recover. For an NLP researcher seeking a grammatical distinction, an unsuccessful feature search leaves several explanations open: the chosen representation, the dictionary’s constraints, the training data, or the encoding procedure. We compare methods by which of these limitations they address. For activation h ∈ ℝ d h\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , an encoder produces z = f θ ​ ( h ) ∈ ℝ m z=f_{\theta}(h)\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and a decoder reconstructs h ^ = b + D ​ z \hat{h}=b+Dz . A common objective is ℒ = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ h − b − D ​ f θ ​ ( h ) ‖ 2 2 + λ ​ Ω ​ ( z ) ] . \mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}[\|h-b-Df_{\theta}(h)\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\Omega(z)]. (1) This objective rewards reconstruction and sparsity; recovering a specified latent structure is a separate endpoint. Synthetic studies can compare against a known generating dictionary, whereas language-model studies must validate the proposed feature interpretation. 3.1 Defining the structure to be recovered The activation site determines the starting object. Residual streams contain accumulated information; attention and MLP outputs characterize component contributions. Transcoders instead approximate a component’s input–output map ( Dunefsky et al., 2024 ; Paulo et al., 2025 ) . Layer transfer, shared dictionaries, and routing change training cost and parameter reuse ( Ghilardi et al., 2024 ; Ghilardi et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) ; comparisons still need to establish what structure is preserved across sites. Within a site, the question is how that structure should be represented. Splitting distributes a concept across latents, while absorption allows a specialized latent to carry a broader property ( Chanin et al., 2025 ) ; neither supports equating an inactive coordinate with absent information. Subspace ( Engels et al., 2025 ; Dalili and Mahdavi, 2026 ) and manifold approaches ( Bhalla et al., 2026a ) model structure beyond individual directions. Nested scales ( Bussmann et al., 2025 ) , parent–child gates ( Muchane et al., 2025 ) , and Kronecker factorization ( Kurochkin et al., 2025 ) impose different forms of organization across features. Temporal smoothness ( Bhalla et al., 2026b ) and predictable-context/novelty separation ( Lubana et al., 2026 ) instead organize variation over sequences. These choices change the candidate unit of analysis: their NLP value depends on whether the resulting directions, groups, or temporal features capture the distinction under study. 3.2 Allocating sparse capacity Once the target is specified, allocation determines which features can participate in each reconstruction. An ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty encourages sparsity but also shrinks amplitudes. Gated SAEs separate selection from magnitude estimation, while JumpReLU learns activation thresholds ( Rajamanoharan et al., 2024a ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024b ) . TopK fixes the number of retained coordinates per input ( Gao et al., 2025 ) ; BatchTopK distributes a budget across a batch and estimates an inference-time threshold ( Bussmann et al., 2024 ) . Top-AFA selects counts through a quasi-orthogonality approximation ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , AdaptiveK uses a learned complexity signal ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , and Group Bias Adaptation (GBA) targets activation-frequency coverage ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . These allocation rules make different assumptions about inputs, geometry, and feature frequency. The results show why allocation cannot be ranked by reconstruction alone. BatchTopK improves reconstruction over TopK, but its Gemma-2-2B comparison with JumpReLU is mixed for downstream cross-entropy degradation ( Bussmann et al., 2024 ) . In GBA’s variable-sparsity synthetic experiment, TopK recovery falls from 98.4% at K = 20 K=20 to 23.4% at K = 50 K=50 ; full versus misspecified frequency coverage gives GBA 100% versus 3.9% recovery ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . These rates use alignment threshold 0.9 and 128 generating features. They demonstrate sensitivity to allocation and coverage assumptions under known ground truth, rather than an NLP ranking. Comparisons should match average sparsity, data, and insertion protocol; decoder normalization must also be recorded because it changes coefficient scales (Appendix C ). 3.3 Separating coverage from inference error Even a suitable representation and budget cannot resolve every failure. Specialized sampling and tilted risk improve access to rare concepts ( Muhamed et al., 2025b ) , changing the training distribution and emphasis of the objective. Weighted SAEs analyze recovery and reweighting under an idealized tied-weight model ( Cui et al., 2026 ) ; those assumptions delimit the result’s applicability to language-model activations. Locally amortized inference addresses a different limitation: a shared encoder can leave an optimization gap relative to per-input sparse coding ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . Improving that approximation does not establish that the reference codes are the intended linguistic features. Thus data coverage, the learning objective, and encoding accuracy require separate comparisons. Answer to RQ1. Recoverability has separable bottlenecks: the representation and its geometry, sparse allocation, training coverage, and inference. The evidence supports diagnosing the suspected bottleneck while matching the remaining conditions. Reconstruction, recovery against a specified reference, and behavioral preservation should remain separate endpoints. Technical comparisons and assumptions are detailed in Appendix C . 4 From Features to Explanations and Mechanisms Claim Weak evidence Moderate evidence Stronger evidence Feature description A label supported only by selected activating examples. The description predicts feature activation on unseen positive and negative examples. Tests with hard negatives and counterexamples; the description distinguishes the feature from similar features. Prediction / diagnosis Correlation observed on training data. Predictive performance on held-out data, compared with a relevant baseline. Generalization and calibration tests; matched supervision and checks for confounding or data leakage. Mechanistic role Feature coactivation or behavioral changes without adequate controls. A targeted intervention produces the predicted behavioral effect. Semantic counterfactuals, reconstruction-error controls, and tests of alternative computational pathways or circuit dependencies. Task control A few selected examples of successful behavior modification. Task improvement over a baseline, with effects on other capabilities assessed. Matched feature-selection and control baselines, with robustness, side effects, and persistence evaluated. Table 1: Evidence supporting different claims about SAE features. Stronger evidence requires more discriminating tests and appropriate controls. The criteria apply to specific claims under stated evaluation conditions, not to the overall quality of a paper. Recovering sparse features leaves their explanatory role unresolved. RQ2 asks what distinguishes a meaningful or useful feature from a faithful account of model computation. A feature may predict sentiment, support sentiment steering, or mediate the model’s own sentiment decision; these claims require different tests. Table 1 organizes support for a specified claim and evaluation setting. Appendix D develops the assessment rules through worked claims and a causal counterexample. 4.1 Testing the feature’s meaning A feature description is a hypothesis about its behavior. Input-oriented descriptions predict what elicits activation; output-oriented descriptions predict contributions to generation ( Gur-Arieh et al., 2025 ) . Automated explanation ( Paulo et al., 2024 ) , agentic testing ( Han et al., 2026 ) , and counterexample-guided revision ( Ma et al., 2025 ) make these hypotheses testable on held-out positives and hard negatives. The critical question is whether the description discriminates the intended property from alternatives. Descriptive collision tests whether one explanation also fits unrelated features ( McCann, 2026 ) ; contrastive stories, semantic/functional neighborhoods, and concept-separability tests examine complementary aspects of specificity ( Gulko et al., 2025 ; Mercorio et al., 2025 ; Fereidouni et al., 2026 ; Härle et al., 2025 ) . The controls must preserve what the claim says should remain invariant. A grammatical feature should track the specified contrast across appropriate lexical controls; a lexical feature need not survive word substitution. Adversarial inputs test the limits of a description ( Li et al., 2026a ) , while randomized SAE components and randomized host models challenge different sources of apparent interpretability ( Korznikov et al., 2026 ; Heap et al., 2026 ) . In the latter comparison, similar aggregate scores in several tested settings show that those metrics need not distinguish learned computations from structure present without training ( Heap et al., 2026 ) . Cross-run consistency asks whether features recur across learned dictionaries ( Song et al., 2026 ) ; recurrence alone does not validate their meaning. 4.2 Testing predictive and causal effects A useful predictor need not identify a variable the source model uses. For a known target, SAE probes should be compared with supervised probes on the original activations, given matched information ( Kantamneni et al., 2025 ; Makelov et al., 2025 ) . For control, direct activation directions provide an alternative ( Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) . These comparisons test the benefit of the SAE representation for the chosen objective. A reusable feature vocabulary can still support exploratory discovery beyond a predefined prediction task ( Peng et al., 2025 ) . Interventions test what changes when a feature is edited. Their effects must be separated from damage introduced by reconstruction. With error e = h − ( b + D ​ z ) e=h-(b+Dz) , an error-preserving edit is h ′ = b + D ​ z ′ + e = h + D ⁡ ( z ′ − z ) . h^{\prime}=b+Dz^{\prime}+e=h+D(z^{\prime}-z). (2) Replacing h h with b + D ​ z ′ b+Dz^{\prime} also removes e e , so the measured effect combines the feature edit with reconstruction error. Retaining e e isolates the decoded change but does not ensure that the edited activation lies within the model’s natural distribution. Null edits, matched-magnitude controls, naturally occurring replacement values, and off-target measurements test distinct alternatives. A controlled effect supports a causal claim about the manipulation; explaining the unmodified computation requires further evidence. 4.3 Testing the proposed mechanism The gap is explicit in Makelov et al. (2024) . Their patching direction combines a concept-correlated component that is disconnected from the output with an ordinarily dormant, output-sensitive component. Patching transfers a signal between them and changes the answer through a route unused before intervention. The successful edit therefore fails to identify the natural mechanism; Appendix D.1 instantiates this counterexample. Conversely, redundant pathways can make a genuinely used feature dispensable under ablation. Necessity and sufficiency must consequently be interpreted relative to the tested interventions and contexts. A circuit claim further specifies dependencies between features. Sparse feature circuits retain feature and error nodes and test task-relevant effects ( Marks et al., 2025 ) . Module-level interventions on coactivation groups ( Deng et al., 2026 ) and transport-based feature matching ( Cao et al., 2026 ) concern group effects and correspondence. Establishing a directed circuit also requires tests of the proposed downstream dependencies; edge attribution helps select candidates for those tests. Attention-output features, formal languages, and Othello models provide distinct computational testbeds whose scope must accompany the interpretation ( Kissane et al., 2024 ; Menon et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024a ) . Neurons, heads, key–value features, and functional dictionaries offer alternative units for the computational account ( O’Neill and Bui, 2024 ; Arora et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Shafran et al., 2026 ; Dunefsky et al., 2024 ) ; the comparison should establish what the SAE basis adds. Answer to RQ2. Semantic interpretability rests on discriminating predictions, and utility on appropriate task comparisons. Mechanistic faithfulness requires evidence that the proposed variables and dependencies capture computation the original model uses. Controlled edits contribute to that assessment, but their success alone does not establish the claimed pathway. A feature can remain useful for control even when its mechanistic interpretation fails. 5 Comparing SAE Usefulness Across NLP Tasks RQ3 asks why NLP studies reach different conclusions about SAE usefulness. The comparison depends on what the task requires, what information the method receives, and which alternative it must outperform. We organize the findings around these differences to identify both useful contributions and the conditions under which their advantages hold. Appendix E provides extended comparisons. 5.1 Objectives change the value of a feature Language identity makes the role of the objective explicit. LangSAE removes language-associated components from pooled multilingual-e5 embeddings for semantic retrieval, whereas CLaS-Bench edits Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to control the output language ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) . Suppressing language identity and strengthening it serve different goals. Their findings concern different task requirements. Within CLaS-Bench, residual difference-in-means scores 84.5 versus 42.3 for SAE difference-in-means, a 42.2-point gap in the combined language/relevance metric ( Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) . The reported selected settings use layers 20 and 25, respectively, both at strength 5. This establishes an advantage for the selected residual-space pipeline; differences in available layers and selection prevent isolating the SAE basis as the cause (Appendix F ). Linguistic analysis asks a more specific question than language control. Language-associated groups support observation and intervention ( Deng et al., 2025 ) ; LinguaLens tests Chinese/English linguistic contrasts ( Jing et al., 2025 ) , while TenseLoC localizes tense and tests English-feature steering ( Tumurchuluun et al., 2025 ) . Script-sensitive representations motivate matched-content and transliteration controls, with raw-neuron interventions serving as a direct comparator ( Verma et al., 2026 ) . Italian-model analysis extends coverage ( Bondielli et al., 2025 ) . Together, these studies motivate testing whether corresponding features preserve a specified linguistic contrast and intervention effect across languages; broad language selectivity or geometric similarity alone does not establish that transfer. 5.2 Representations and baselines define the comparison Classification provides a concrete reconciliation. Positive Gemma results compare SAE classifiers with last-token hidden-state baselines ( Gallifant et al., 2025 ) . In sparse probing, adding attention-pooled dense baselines reduces the apparent advantage of pooled SAE probes ( Kantamneni et al., 2025 ) . Both studies examine pooling, so its presence alone cannot explain their disagreement. The within-study comparison establishes that baseline construction matters; attributing all cross-paper differences to it would require matching the model, data, feature selection, and classifier. Task-aligned classification additionally changes representation training ( Bail et al., 2025 ) . DILA and topic modeling construct interpretable task systems ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) , rather than explaining an unchanged source model. Speech analysis, vision–language alignment, and multimodal tracing further change the representation being examined ( Pluth et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; DHIMOÏLA et al., 2026 ; Kaushik et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . These extensions require comparisons appropriate to acoustic frames, visual embeddings, or text tokens. 5.3 Information access separates RAG outcomes Retrieval-oriented objectives can preserve useful matching structure ( Kang et al., 2025 ) , while adapting a retriever around a frozen dictionary constructs a new retrieval system ( Formal et al., 2026 ) . For retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), improvements concern different stages: detecting unsupported output, choosing between context and memory, enriching a query, or repairing an answer. Table 2 distinguishes these operations and their information requirements. A detector can identify errors without explaining their cause, and increased reliance on context helps only when that context is trustworthy. SAE use Information used Reported contribution Key evaluation distinction Hallucination detection and feedback ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Xiong et al., 2026 ) Sparse features and detection signals; feedback adds a generation stage. Detect unsupported answers and guide subsequent generation. Evaluate detection and generation improvements separately. Context–memory selection ( Xin et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025b ) Features identified through contrasts between retrieved context and internal knowledge. Change which information source the model relies on. Measure source preference and answer correctness separately. Query enrichment ( Abdaljalil et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) SAE-guided query modifications; some analyses select successful query expansions. Improve retrieval/generation or analyze query-expansion effects. Test on unselected queries and evaluate the contribution of the SAE within the full pipeline. Distractor repair ( Giannetti et al., 2026 ) Known correct answer token used to optimize latent activations on selected difficult examples. Recover answers affected by distracting documents. Distinguish oracle-assisted repair from autonomous error correction. Table 2: Comparison of SAE-based approaches to RAG. The methods differ in their objectives, available information, and evaluation settings; their reported improvements therefore do not measure the same capability. LatDefuse illustrates why information access belongs in the comparison. It optimizes latent edits toward a known correct token at answer divergence and evaluates distractor-vulnerable instances ( Giannetti et al., 2026 ) . The result establishes conditional repair capacity. Comparing its recovery rate directly with autonomous detection or correction would conflate different supervision and evaluation populations. An integrated system would need to evaluate detection, source arbitration, and repair together, including errors passed between stages. 5.4 Selection and prompts shape instruction gains For reasoning, steering a strategy and identifying its computation are separate achievements. Reasoning-associated features can change traces or strategies ( Galichin et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) , while cue-injection and meaning-preserving tests can challenge an abstract-reasoning label ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . Temporal-difference analysis ties features to specified computational variables in an in-context reinforcement-learning task ( Demircan et al., 2025 ) . These findings answer different questions about control, feature meaning, and computation; lexical cues must be varied independently of the required operation to compare those claims. Instruction methods also differ in how they select features: SAIF identifies instruction-related features ( He et al., 2025 ) , narrative editing generates compliant/violating contrasts ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) , SISTER uses prompt variation ( Cho and Hockenmaier, 2025 ) , and PULSE uses labeled demonstration utility ( Hao et al., 2026 ) . Comparators need access to the same signals. Evaluation prompts matter as well: for Gemma-2-2B sentiment circuits, SST-2 F1 gains are 37.19 points under template T1 and 2.96 under T4 ( Li et al., 2026b ) . These three-run mean differences establish prompt dependence within the reported setting; they do not isolate baseline headroom as its cause. The stage of use changes the comparison further. Concept-based pretraining ( Tack et al., 2026 ) and feature-guided fine-tuning data selection ( Shi et al., 2026 ) construct changed models; transfer prediction ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) and sparse model diffing ( Kassem et al., 2025 ) respectively anticipate and diagnose updates. Inference-time activation or input edits leave weights fixed; diffusion-language analyses additionally depend on denoising time and mask position ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . 5.5 Controllers determine regulation trade-offs Behavioral regulation tests what the complete intervention achieves. Refusal-feature analysis and adversarial detection ( Yeo et al., 2025 ) concern different outcomes from maintaining benign capabilities during control. Static refusal amplification can impair unrelated capabilities ( O’Brien et al., 2024 ) ; REINS and graph-regularized steering combine selected directions with runtime gating ( Ding et al., 2026 ; Yeon et al., 2025 ) . Their comparison therefore involves both the feature directions and the decision about when to intervene. Unlearning makes this distinction concrete. Static suppression has mixed multi-topic results ( Farrell et al., 2024 ) ; Dynamic SAE Guardrails add input-dependent classification ( Muhamed et al., 2025a ) , whereas subspace-guided projection and CRISP modify parameters ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Ashuach et al., 2026 ) . Conditional intervention can avoid unnecessary edits, while parameter updates remove dependence on a runtime controller. Comparing their forget–retain trade-offs requires matching target knowledge, evaluation populations, retention tasks, and relearning attacks. Adaptation constraints ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Peng et al., 2026 ) and backdoor analyses ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Antoun et al., 2026 ) add further training and attack conditions. These differences identify what a controlled comparison must hold fixed before attributing a gain to the dictionary. Answer to RQ3. SAE usefulness depends on the objective, representation, comparison baseline, available supervision, and intervention pipeline. Opposing treatments of language identity can both serve their respective tasks; classification, repair, and regulation results require matching the conditions defining success. The synthesis reconciles the scope of these findings. Establishing which factor causes a remaining performance difference requires experiments that vary it while controlling the others. 6 Research Directions and Practical Choices The answers to RQ1–RQ3 identify recovery bottlenecks, requirements for mechanistic claims, and conditions shaping task utility. They motivate experiments that distinguish competing explanations and guide the choice of an appropriate unit of analysis. 6.1 Three testable comparisons Discourse structure versus temporal persistence. Compare static and temporal dictionaries with matched host model, layer, capacity, average sparsity, and training corpus ( Bhalla et al., 2026b ; Lubana et al., 2026 ) . Vary semantic continuity, lexical repetition, and abrupt discourse change independently. Measure held-out contrast discrimination and predicted intervention effects on entity/state tracking. This tests whether temporal structure captures discourse-relevant distinctions beyond lexical persistence; smooth codes and separate task gains would leave that relationship unresolved. Feature matching versus intervention transfer. Match features across random seeds, paraphrases, and languages using geometry and activation distributions, then test whether correspondence predicts preservation of an independently specified intervention effect. Include unmatched and frequency-matched controls. Current consistency and matching measures ( Song et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2026 ) motivate these comparisons, while known-concept disentanglement results ( Mueller et al., 2026b ) motivate testing functional roles separately. Selection and controller versus dictionary. With fixed train/validation/test splits, cross SAE dictionaries with shared supervised or unsupervised selection rules and static or gated controllers. Include dense probes for prediction and direct-space directions for control, with matched labels and tuning budgets. Report the target–retention frontier. The probing/classification disagreement and conditional-control advances motivate this design; attributing their differences to selection or gating remains a hypothesis until those factors are controlled. 6.2 Choosing when an SAE adds value For a known predictive target, begin with a well-tuned supervised probe and a matched label budget. For output control, include direct activation directions before incurring dictionary-training and feature-selection costs. For a localized computational hypothesis, neurons, heads, or a functional surrogate may provide the required unit. Direct comparators support these choices ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Arora et al., 2026 ; Shafran et al., 2026 ; Gurgurov et al., 2026 ) . An SAE is more compelling when a reusable, fine-grained feature vocabulary enables discovery, comparison across many questions, or a demonstrated specificity/cost advantage. 7 Conclusion This survey critically examines the role of sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability and NLP. Through a task-grounded taxonomy of dictionary design, feature operations, and NLP functions, we identify key challenges in feature recoverability, distinguish semantic interpretability from mechanistic faithfulness, and explain how task objectives and experimental pipelines shape reported utility. Our comparative synthesis reconciles apparent disagreements across studies and highlights where matched evaluations remain necessary. These findings provide NLP researchers with a framework for evaluating SAE contributions, selecting appropriate baselines, and determining whether useful features also explain the model’s underlying computations. Limitations This survey focuses on sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability and their applications to natural language processing. It does not aim to comprehensively cover related developments in sparse coding, disentangled representation learning, or interpretability methods beyond SAEs. Given the rapid evolution of this research area, our synthesis reflects the literature available within the survey’s defined scope. Comparisons across studies are constrained by differences in model architectures, datasets, feature representations, and evaluation protocols. Accordingly, our analyses emphasize the conditions under which findings are supported rather than establishing universal rankings of SAE methods. The proposed taxonomy and evidence framework provide a basis for future comparative evaluations, including controlled experiments across NLP tasks.
